newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU begins new push to woo Chinese trade.
newsitem.headline: EU begins new push to woo Chinese trade.

text.p: European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan begins a visit to China this week during which he will unveil measures aimed at helping EU firms tap into what is potentially the world's biggest market.
Brittan heads a delegation of more than 30 European business leaders representing industries ranging from telecoms and television to aviation and insurance.
"This is a very, very important visit," Brittan told a news conference before leaving for China. "There is no question of us underestimating China's importance to world trade."

The EU's mission, which begins on Thursday, will focus on tapping into China's lucrative television, insurance, aviation and telecoms industries, but officials said it will look also at environmental, technical and industrial training.

Brittan said he would "most certainly" raise the question of China's efforts to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO) during the visit and was looking for a clear signal that Beijing was prepared to abide by WTO rules.

"There are clear signs of readiness and I will urge them to accelerate the process," he said. "I am looking for China to say 'Yes, we accept the basic concept and are taking on the obligations of negotiating WTO membership'."

Brittan will not, however, be travelling with a message of cheer for Beijing officials hoping for a change in the Commission's anti-dumping policy -- an area in which China feels it is particularly hard-hit.

While the Commission was prepared to make some concessions in individual cases, Brittan said there would be no change in its "analog market" policy. Under this anti-dumping tariffs are calculated by comparing the production costs of goods from non-market economies with products from market economy countries.

China and many non-market economies, countries where there is no real consumers for the product, complain this is like comparing apples with pears as their labour costs are compared with those in the developed world when calculating anti-dumping duties.
Brittan said one area where the EU was hoping for substantial progress was in cracking down on the abuse of intellectual property rights.

Included in the delegation are officials from the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) who last week said Chinese trade practices were substantially hampering their activities.
"International investment and the development of a legitimate music market in China remain strictly limited by lack of market access and by piracy," the organisation said.
However, the IFPI said there had been "sporadic evidence" that some anti-piracy efforts were working.
The desire to tap into China's markets has been criticised by human rights organisations who want the Commission to put more emphasis on encouraging democracy.

Percy Westerlund, director of the Commission's relations with Asia, said Brittan would not hesitate to raise the subject during his visit. "Sir Leon has never drawn back from raising such issues at the appropriate times," he said.
Among the firms included in the delegation are EMI Polygram, Prudential, Airbus Industrie, Nokia, Stet, British Telecom, SAAB, Aerospatiale and Dresdner Bank.
